body.p: The Examiner has rejected claims 1-3, 5-10, 17-19, 21-26, 31, and 45 under 35 U.S.C. §101 as allegedly being drawn to non-statutory subject matter; rejected claims 1, 17, 31, and 45 alleged that the claims would be construed under 35 U.S.C. §112(f) as means or step plus function; rejected claims 1-3, 17-19, 31, and 45 under 35 U.S.C. §102(a)(2) as allegedly being anticipated by U.S. Patent Publication No. 2020/0110194 to Young et al. ("Young"); rejected claims 5-8 and 21-24 under 35 U.S.C. §103 as allegedly being unpatentably obvious over Young in view of U.S. Patent Publication No. 2005/0124864 to Mack et al. ("Mack"); rejected claims 9 and 25 under 35 U.S.C. §103 as allegedly being unpatentably obvious over Young in view of U.S. Patent Publication No. 2020/0146910 to Demirli et al. ("Demirli"); rejected claims 10 and 26 under 35 U.S.C. §103 as allegedly being unpatentably obvious over Young in view of U.S. Patent Publication No. 2014/037163 5 to Shinar et al. ("Shinar").

Summary of Amendments. With this amendment, claims 1, 6, 17, 22, 31, and 45 have been amended, and claims 5 and 21 have been cancelled without prejudice or disclaimer. The amendments and new claims are fully supported by the original specification as indicated below. Claim Rejections Under 35 U.S.C. 101

Claims 1-3, 5-10, 17-19, 21-26, 31, and 45 stand rejected under 35 U.S.C. §101, because the Office alleges that the claims are drawn to unpatentable subject matter. This rejection is respectfully traversed.
The Examiner acknowledges that "claims 1-3, 5-10, 17-19, 21-26, 31, and 45 ... [are] directed to statutory subject matter." Office Action, p. 5. However, the Examiner alleges that "the
recited steps [of claims 1, 17, 31, and 45] are directed to mathematical calculations and/or mental processes of performing concepts by a human..." Id. Applicant respectfully disagrees.

Claim 1 cannot be practically performed by a human mind. Here, like in SRI International, Inc. v. Cisco Systems, Inc. (Fed. Cir. 2019)1, the human mind is not meant to transform, in response to a change in the force data indicative of a change in a load on the article and based on a determination of a plurality of physiological sources on the article, the force data from each of the plurality of sensors into a corresponding plurality of physiological signals ... wherein transforming the force data comprises time-domain and/or frequency- domain filtering the force data to obtain a plurality of respiratory signals corresponding to each of the plurality of sensors.2 See also SiRF Tech., Inc. v. Int'l Trade Comm 'n, 601 F.3d 1319, 94 USPQ2d 1607 (Fed. Cir. 2010) (where a claim to a method for calculating an absolute position of a GPS receiver and an absolute time of reception of satellite signals, where the claimed GPS receiver calculated pseudoranges that estimated the distance from the GPS receiver to a plurality of satellites was found to NOT be mental steps and as such patent eligible).
Unlike CyberSource, it would be unreasonable to allege that a human mind or a human with pen and paper can perform the following as required by claim 1:
receive, from the communication module, the force data;

transform, in response to a change in the force data indicative of a change in a load on the article and based on a determination of a plurality of physiological sources on the article, the force data from each of the plurality of sensors into a
corresponding plurality of physiological signals; and
1 CyberSource Corp. v. Retail Decisions, Inc., 654 F.3d 1366, 1372, 99 USPQ2d 1690, 1695 (Fed. Cir. 2011).

2 See SRIInt'l, Inc. v. Cisco Systems, Inc., 930 F.3d 1295, 1304 (Fed. Cir. 2019) (declining to identify the claimed collection and analysis of network data as abstract because "the human mind is not equipped to detect suspicious activity by using network monitors and analyzing network packets as recited by the claims").
determine, based on the plurality of physiological signals, a source physiological signal for each of the plurality of physiological sources;
wherein the determination of the source physiological signal for each of the plurality of physiological sources comprises:

separating into components each of the plurality of physiological signals, wherein the components correspond to each of the plurality of physiological sources at each of the plurality of sensors; and compositing the separated components for each of the plurality of physiological sources, wherein the compositing forms the source physiological signal for each of the plurality of physiological sources, and wherein transforming the force data comprises time-domain or frequency-domain filtering the force data to obtain a plurality of respiratory signals corresponding to each of the plurality of sensors.3

With respect to mathematical processes, claim 1 does NOT recite mathematical formulas, calculations, or formulas, but rather the application of transformations of data. Indeed, the MPEP explains "[t]hat a mathematical equation [] required to complete the claimed method and system does not doom the claims to abstraction." MPEP 2106 (citing also Thales Visionix Inc. v. United States, 850 F.3d. 1343, 1349, 121 USPQ2d 1898, 1902 (Fed. Cir. 2017)).

Furthermore, claim 1 relates to practical application of technology, rather than an abstract idea or mental steps. Specifically, claim 1 provides computer-implemented technology that processes and transforms data to provide a respiratory signal. The use of such technology cannot be fairly read on or alleged to be mental steps as alleged by the Examiner.

For at least the above-noted reasons, claim 1 is patentable subject matter. Accordingly, the rejection under 35 U.S.C. §101 of claim 1 (as well as the corresponding dependent claims) should be withdrawn.
Independent claims 17, 31, and 45 include features substantially similar to those discussed above with respect to claim 1. For at least the reasons noted with respect to claim 1, claims 17, 31,
3 Underline indicates newly added language
and 45 are directed to patentable subject matter. Accordingly, the rejection under 35 U. S. C. §101 of claims 17, 31, and 45 (as well as the corresponding dependent claims) should be withdrawn.
For at least these reasons, withdrawal of the pending rejection under 35 U.S.C. §101 is respectfully requested.

The Examiner has apparently interpreted the claims under 35 U.S.C. § 112 (f) as means or step plus function. In particular, the Examiner has invoked interpretation under 35 U.S.C. §112 (f) in interpretating the claimed "communications module" and "remote processing device." Office Action, p. 4.
Applicant respectfully traverses this interpretation of the claims.

Regarding the claimed "communications module," claims 1, 17, 31, and 45 have been amended to recite, inter alia, "a communication module in wired communication with a plurality of sensors" (emphasis added). Claims 1, 17, 31, and 45 thus recite sufficient structure surrounding the claimed "communication module" to perform the allegedly claimed functions, and should not be interpreted under 35 U.S.C. §112 (f).
For at least these reasons, Applicant respectfully requests that the Examiner not interpret the claims under 35 U.S.C. §112 (f).

Claims 1-3, 17-19, 31, and 45 stand rejected under 35 U.S.C. §102(a)(2) as allegedly being anticipated by Young. Claims 5-8 and 21-24 stand rejected under 35 U.S.C. §103 as allegedly being unpatentably obvious over Young in view of Mack. The remaining claims stand rejected
under pre-A.IA. 35 U.S.C. §103 as being unpatentable over Young as combined with other
references. These rejections are respectfully traversed.
To advance prosecution, claim 1 has been amended to recite the features of now-cancelled
claim 5. Claim 1 as amended recites a system comprising:
a plurality of sensors, each of the plurality of sensors configured to engage with an article on which a first user is positioned, and each of the plurality of sensors configured to measure force;
a communication module in communication with each of the plurality of sensors, wherein
the communication module receives force data transmitted from each of the plurality of sensors; and
an apparatus comprising:
at least one data processor; and
at least one memory storing instructions which, when executed by the at least one
data processor, cause the apparatus to at least:
receive, from the communication module, the force data;

transform, in response to a change in the force data indicative of a change in a load on the article and based on a determination of a plurality of physiological sources on the article, the force data from each of the plurality of sensors into a
corresponding plurality of physiological signals; and
determine, based on the plurality of physiological signals, a source physiological signal for each of the plurality of physiological sources;
wherein the determination of the source physiological signal for each of the plurality of physiological sources comprises:

separating into components each of the plurality of physiological signals, wherein the components correspond to each of the plurality of physiological sources at each of the plurality of sensors; and compositing the separated components for each of the plurality of physiological sources, wherein the compositing forms the source physiological signal for each of the plurality of physiological sources, and wherein transforming the force data comprises time-domain or frequency-domain filtering the force data to obtain a plurality of respiratory signals corresponding to each of the plurality of sensors.4
Neither Young nor Mack discloses or suggests at least the underlined features of amended
claim 1. In rejecting claim 5, the Examiner refers to paragraph [0063] of Mack and alleges that "it
would have been obvious to one of ordinary skill in the art ... to have modified Young by
incorporating the teachings of Mack by utilizing frequency-domain filtering to transform the force
a Underline indicates newly added language

data into respiratory signals and to do this for each of the plurality of sensors." Office Action, p. 17. Applicant disagrees, as a POSITA would not have been motivated to combine Young and Mack for at least the reasons noted below.5

Mack at paragraph [0063] and elsewhere is silent with respect to "transforming the force data [via] time-domain or frequency-domain filtering [of] the force data to obtain a plurality of respiratory signals corresponding to each of the plurality of sensors," as amended claim 1 recites (emphasis added). Young is similarly silent with respect to transformation of data "to obtain a plurality of respiratory signals corresponding to each of the plurality of sensors." Young, taken alone or in combination with Mack, thus fails to teach or suggest the features of amended claim 1. For at least these reasons, a POSITA would not be motivated to modify Young's teachings based on those of Mack, as the Examiner alleges.

In view of the forgoing, claim 1 is not anticipated by Young. Claims 2 and 3 depend from claim 1, and are thus not anticipated by Young by virtue of their dependencies at least. Claims 6-8, which stand rejected as being allegedly obvious in view of Young and Mack, depend either directly or indirectly from claim 1, and are thus patentable over Young, taken alone or in combination with Mack, by virtue of their dependencies at least. As discussed, the features of claim 5 have been incorporated into claim 1, and claim 5 has been cancelled without prejudice or disclaimer. The rejection of claim 5 over Young in view of Mack is thus moot.
Claim 9 stands rejected as being allegedly unpatentable over Young in view of Demirli. Demirli does not remedy the deficiencies in the combination of Young and Mack, discussed above.

Claim 9 depends from claim 1, and is thus patentable over Young, taken alone or in combination with either or both of Mack and Demirli, by virtue of its dependency at least.

Claim 10 stands rejected as being allegedly unpatentable over Young in view of Shinar. Shinar does not remedy the deficiencies in the combination of Young and Mack, discussed above. Claim 10 depends from claim 1, and is thus patentable over Young, taken alone or in combination with either or both of Mack and Shinar, by virtue of its dependency at least.

Claims 17, 31, and 45 have been amended to recite features substantially similar to those of claim 1 discussed above. Claims 17, 31, and 45 are thus patentable over Young, taken alone or in combination with Mack, for at least the reasons discussed above with respect to claim 1. Claims 18, 19, and 22-26 depend, either directly or indirectly, from claim 17, and are thus patentable over Young, taken alone or in combination with any or all of Mack, Demirli, and Shinar, by virtue of their dependencies at least.

On the basis of the foregoing amendments, the pending claims are in condition for allowance. It is believed that all of the pending claims have been addressed in this paper. However, failure to address a specific rejection, issue or comment, does not signify agreement with or concession of that rejection, issue or comment. In addition, because the arguments made above are not intended to be exhaustive, there may be reasons for patentability of any or all pending claims (or other claims) that have not been expressed. Finally, nothing in this paper should be construed as an intent to concede any issue with regard to any claim, except as specifically stated in this paper.

No additional fees are believed to be due other than those for the three-month extension of time. However, the Commissioner is hereby authorized to charge any additional fees that may be due, or credit any overpayment of same, to Deposit Account 50-0311, Reference No. 37866- 639N01US/2018-330-2.
